Nuclear Espionage. During the Manhattan Project and beyond, the Soviet Union made nuclear secrets its single highest intelligence objective. Soviet intelligence services deployed dozens of agents to penetrate American and British scientific laboratories and military installations, recruiting scientists, technicians, and sympathizers who provided designs, manufacturing methods, and test data that accelerated Soviet atomic capabilities.

Klaus Fuchs was a German-born British physicist who passed detailed information about bomb design and plutonium production directly to Soviet handlers, significantly advancing Soviet weapons development. In the United States, Julius Rosenberg, an electrical engineer at Los Alamos, coordinated a ring of spies including his wife Ethel, his brother-in-law David Greenglass, and others, stealing weapons designs and test data. The Rosenbergs were executed in 1953, the only US civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. This punishment reflected both the era's security hysteria and genuine damage to American security.

Soviet acquisition of nuclear technology through espionage compressed the timeline dramatically. The Soviet Union achieved atomic weapons in 1949 and thermonuclear weapons in 1953, intensifying superpower arms race anxiety. These successes exposed the vulnerability of scientific institutions to recruitment and betrayal, leading to rigorous security clearances, compartmentalization, and security cultures that persisted throughout the Cold War and beyond. The most famous cases became symbols of Cold War security anxieties and ideological betrayal.
